items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No script was saved. All logic ran as one-off `python3 -c` blobs with cryptic names (`dec`, `wal`, `r[0]`, `b`) and almost no comments. The final step `bytes([b ^ 0x42 for b in encrypted_wal])` sits inline in a shell command.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The conventions ask for a small re-runnable decrypt script plus an extraction step. The agent left only recovered.json and a modified WAL; the decrypt and extract logic ran in a single throwaway `python3 -c` (step 31). Checksum code was copy-pasted across steps 10–12.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final in-place write hardcodes `0x42` and does not check the magic or frame checksums before overwriting /app/main.db-wal. There is no error handling. Files are opened with `with` and an earlier dry run validated the approach.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: Derived the key by XORing the header with the expected magic 377f0682 (key 0x42). Verified the header and every frame checksum (`All frames valid? True`). Let SQLite replay the WAL on copies in /tmp, then checked all 11 records.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Copied the original DB and WAL to /root/wal_backup (chmod 444) and did all tests on /tmp copies before the in-place decrypt. Minor issue: it later ran `rm -rf /root/wal_backup`, deleting that backup.
